title: Fear Extinction
subtitle: Learning safety without deleting the old association
altText: Chalkboard-style clinical neuroscience diagram illustrating fear extinction across threat, memory, regulation and treatment systems.
learningObjectives: Explain fear extinction in clinically accurate language.
Distinguish established findings from theoretical or mixed claims in fear extinction.
Identify one limitation or safety implication relevant to fear extinction.

sections.explainSimply: Extinction creates new learning that a cue can be safe in the present.
sections.explainLikePsychologist: The original threat memory usually remains available, which helps explain renewal, reinstatement and spontaneous recovery.
sections.advancedClinicalDetail: Exposure works best when it supports expectancy violation, variability, context generalisation and reduced safety behaviours.
sections.thinkOfItLike: Think of fear extinction as one part of a dynamic safety-and-learning system rather than a single switch.
sections.whyPsychologistsCare: Psychologists need fear extinction to connect symptoms with learning, context, risk and treatment choice without reducing the person to a brain scan.
sections.whenItGoesWrong: A temporary return of fear does not mean treatment failed.
sections.clinicalPearl: Clinical pearl: use fear extinction to sharpen formulation, not to replace phenomenology or outcome measurement.
sections.practicalExample: A clinician uses fear extinction to formulate triggers, state shifts, avoidance and functional impact, then monitors whether intervention improves daily life rather than relying on presumed neural change.
sections.limitationsCautions: A temporary return of fear does not mean treatment failed. Evidence classification: established learning mechanism.
